title: Banach–Steinhaus Divergence Principle (engine of du Bois-Reymond)
description: Turns the parent's Banach–Steinhaus resonance statement into a divergence statement: a sequence of bounded operators with unbounded operator norms has a point whose orbit fails to converge (and is in fact unbounded). Specialised to scalar functionals this is the abstract engine of du Bois-Reymond's theorem on divergent Fourier series — given the (Mathlib-absent) unboundedness of the Lebesgue constants, the partial-sum functionals on C(𝕋) produce a continuous function with divergent Fourier series. The unconditional Fourier result is NOT claimed; the Lebesgue-constant growth is left as an explicit, documented hypothesis.

meta.author: Lean Genius
meta.assumptions: No axioms (#print axioms reports only propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound). The headline du Bois-Reymond instantiation is CONDITIONAL: the theorem exists_divergent_partialSums takes the unboundedness of the partial-sum operator norms (the Lebesgue constants) as an explicit hypothesis. That hypothesis is the classical fact ∫|D_n| ∼ log n → ∞, which is not yet formalised in Mathlib; consequently the UNCONDITIONAL existence of a continuous function with a divergent Fourier series is not claimed by this entry. Everything actually proved is a true, unconditional theorem about families of operators with unbounded norms.
originalContributions: exists_divergent_orbit_of_unbounded_opNorm: unbounded operator norms ⟹ a point x at which the orbit n ↦ T n x does NOT converge — upgrades the parent's resonance (unboundedness) to non-convergence
exists_divergent_orbit_unbounded: the same resonance point has an unbounded orbit (∀ C, ∃ n, C < ‖T n x‖) — the strong divergence witness

exists_divergent_partialSums: the scalar / Fourier-shaped form — functionals S n : V →L[ℂ] ℂ with unbounded norms yield f with S n f non-convergent; this is the faithful Banach–Steinhaus half of du Bois-Reymond
exists_bound_of_tendsto: the elementary bridge (a convergent sequence is norm-bounded) that converts resonance into divergence

overview.historicalContext: In 1873 Paul du Bois-Reymond constructed a continuous 2π-periodic function whose Fourier series diverges at a point, demolishing the widespread expectation that continuity guarantees pointwise Fourier convergence. The modern proof, due to Lebesgue and crystallised by the Banach–Steinhaus theorem (1927), is a textbook application of the Uniform Boundedness Principle: the Fourier partial-sum functionals S_n : C(𝕋) → ℂ, f ↦ S_n f(0), have operator norms equal to the Lebesgue constants L_n = (1/2π)∫|D_n|, where D_n is the Dirichlet kernel; since L_n ∼ (4/π²) log n → ∞, the family is not uniformly bounded, and Banach–Steinhaus resonance produces a continuous function at which the partial sums are unbounded — hence divergent. This entry isolates the abstract engine of that argument: the step from 'unbounded operator norms' to 'a point of genuine divergence (non-convergence)'. The parent entry supplies resonance (pointwise unboundedness); the contribution here is that unboundedness of an orbit rules out convergence, which is the form a divergence theorem actually needs.
overview.problemStatement:
**OQ-01-OQ-01-OQ-02 of baire-category-theorem**

Apply the resonance principle exists_resonance_of_not_uniformly_bounded to the Fourier partial-sum operators to obtain a continuous function with a divergent Fourier series (du Bois-Reymond).
overview.text: Unbounded operator norms ⟹ a point with non-convergent orbit; specialised to Fourier partial-sum functionals (given unbounded Lebesgue constants), a continuous function with divergent Fourier series.
overview.proofStrategy:
**Two moves.**
1. **Resonance ⟹ divergence**: From the parent resonance theorem, unbounded operator norms give a point x with sup_n ‖T n x‖ = ∞. A convergent sequence in a normed space has bounded range (Metric.isBounded_range_of_tendsto + isBounded_iff_forall_norm_le, packaged as exists_bound_of_tendsto), so the orbit n ↦ T n x cannot converge. This yields exists_divergent_orbit_of_unbounded_opNorm and, by unfolding the unbounded witness, exists_divergent_orbit_unbounded.
2. **Fourier shape**: Specialising F = ℂ gives exists_divergent_partialSums for functionals S : ℕ → V →L[ℂ] ℂ. Instantiating V = C(𝕋) and S n = (f ↦ S_n f(0)) with the (classical, Mathlib-absent) unboundedness of the Lebesgue constants discharges the hypothesis and produces du Bois-Reymond's divergent-Fourier function.
keyInsights: Resonance is about *unboundedness* of an orbit; divergence is about *non-convergence*. The bridge is one line of analysis: a convergent sequence is bounded, so an unbounded orbit cannot converge. This small step is precisely what makes the Banach–Steinhaus argument deliver a DIVERGENT (not merely large) Fourier series.

The whole Fourier-specific difficulty is concentrated in a single scalar quantity: the operator norm ‖S n‖ = Lebesgue constant L_n. Once L_n → ∞ is known, the existence of a divergent-Fourier continuous function is a pure soft-analysis consequence with no further Fourier input — which is exactly the division of labour this entry formalises.

Honesty boundary: the Lebesgue-constant growth ∫|D_n| ∼ log n is NOT in Mathlib (no Dirichlet kernel / Lebesgue constant development), so the entry proves the conditional reduction and explicitly flags the unconditional du Bois-Reymond statement as open. The conditionality lives in an ordinary hypothesis, not an axiom, so every stated theorem is unconditionally true.

The abstract theorems are stated for general Banach E and normed F (and the Fourier corollary for complex Banach V), so they are reusable for any Banach–Steinhaus divergence argument (e.g. divergent Lagrange interpolation, unbounded quadrature error), not only Fourier series.

exists_divergent_partialSums adds no new proof content beyond specialisation: its body is the one-line term-mode application `exists_divergent_orbit_of_unbounded_opNorm hUnbdd` at F := ℂ, not a fresh `by` proof. All the mathematical work — resonance, then the bounded-range bridge — is discharged once in exists_divergent_orbit_of_unbounded_opNorm; the 'Fourier form' is purely a specialisation of the general operator statement, not an independent argument.
prerequisites: Basic normed-space facts: a convergent sequence has bounded range
Operator norm and the contrapositive Uniform Boundedness Principle

sections.title: Module Header and Imports
sections.summary: Extensive docstring stating what is proved (the abstract divergence principle and its scalar Fourier form), the du Bois-Reymond instantiation, and an explicit honesty note that the unconditional divergent-Fourier result is not claimed (the Lebesgue-constant growth is Mathlib-absent and enters as a hypothesis). Imports Mathlib and the parent Proofs.BaireCategoryTheoremOQ01OQ01; opens Filter, Topology and the parent namespace.
sections.mathContext: Sets up a Banach space $E$, normed space $F$, and the parent's resonance theorem $\neg(\exists C,\ \forall i,\ \|g_i\| \le C) \Rightarrow \exists x,\ \neg(\exists C,\ \forall i,\ \|g_i x\| \le C)$.

sections.title: Convergent ⟹ Bounded
sections.summary: Variable block (Banach space E, normed space F) and lemma exists_bound_of_tendsto: a convergent sequence y n → L admits a uniform bound ‖y n‖ ≤ C. Uses Metric.isBounded_range_of_tendsto to bound the range, then isBounded_iff_forall_norm_le to extract C.
sections.mathContext: A convergent sequence in a normed space is bounded. This is the single analytic fact that turns resonance (unbounded orbit) into divergence (no limit).

sections.title: The Divergence Principle
sections.summary: Theorem exists_divergent_orbit_of_unbounded_opNorm: unbounded operator norms ⟹ a point x with n ↦ T n x non-convergent. Extracts the parent's resonance point, then rules out a limit via exists_bound_of_tendsto — a convergent orbit would be bounded, contradicting resonance.
sections.mathContext: Resonance gives $\sup_n \|T_n x\| = \infty$; since a convergent sequence is bounded, $(T_n x)$ can have no limit.

sections.title: The Unbounded-Orbit Witness
sections.summary: Theorem exists_divergent_orbit_unbounded: the resonance point x has, in fact, an unbounded orbit — ∀ C, ∃ n, C < ‖T n x‖ — the strong divergence witness with no finite envelope. Proved by by_contra + push_neg, feeding the negated bound back into the resonance witness.
sections.mathContext: For every $C$ some $\|T_n x\|$ exceeds $C$: the orbit escapes every bound, strictly stronger than mere non-convergence.

sections.title: du Bois-Reymond Reduction (Scalar Form)
sections.summary: Theorem exists_divergent_partialSums: for functionals S : ℕ → V →L[ℂ] ℂ on a complex Banach space with unbounded norms, there is f with S n f non-convergent. Documented as the V = C(𝕋), S n f = n-th Fourier partial sum at 0 instantiation; the unbounded-norm hypothesis is the Lebesgue-constant growth.
sections.mathContext: Specialising $F = \mathbb{C}$ yields the form matching Fourier partial sums: $\|S_n\| = L_n$ (Lebesgue constants), and $L_n \to \infty$ produces a continuous function with a Fourier series divergent at $0$.

crossReferences.description: Parent: derives Banach–Steinhaus / Uniform Boundedness and the resonance statement exists_resonance_of_not_uniformly_bounded from the gallery Baire theorem. This entry upgrades resonance (pointwise unboundedness) to non-convergence (divergence).
Grandparent: the Baire category theorem on complete metric spaces, the foundation of the Uniform Boundedness Principle.
Sibling open-question branch off the same Baire/Banach–Steinhaus development.

conclusion.summary: Machine-verified: a sequence of bounded operators with unbounded operator norms has a point whose orbit does not converge (and is unbounded). Specialised to scalar functionals this is the abstract engine of du Bois-Reymond's divergent-Fourier theorem; instantiating with the Fourier partial-sum functionals on C(𝕋) and the classical unboundedness of the Lebesgue constants yields a continuous function with divergent Fourier series. Zero sorries, zero axioms. The unconditional Fourier statement is left open, contingent on formalising the Lebesgue-constant growth.
conclusion.implications: **Reusable divergence engine**: any Banach–Steinhaus divergence argument (Fourier series, Lagrange interpolation at equispaced nodes, quadrature error) reduces to checking that the relevant operator norms are unbounded; the soft-analysis half is now a one-line application.\n\n**Sharp division of labour**: the entry makes explicit that du Bois-Reymond = (Banach–Steinhaus, done here) + (Lebesgue constants → ∞, the analytic core still missing from Mathlib).
openQuestions: Formalise the Dirichlet kernel D_n(t) = sin((n+½)t)/sin(t/2) and prove the Lebesgue-constant lower bound (1/2π)∫_{-π}^{π}|D_n(t)| dt ≥ c·log n (e.g. via |sin| ≥ (2/π)·(t/π) on [0,π] and the harmonic-sum estimate). This is the missing analytic core.

Package the Fourier partial-sum-at-0 map S n : C(AddCircle 1) →L[ℂ] ℂ, S n f = ∑_{|k|≤n} fourierCoeff f k, as a continuous linear functional (the coefficient bound |fourierCoeff f k| ≤ ‖f‖ over the probability Haar measure makes each summand a CLM), and prove ‖S n‖ equals the Lebesgue constant.
Combine the two preceding items with exists_divergent_partialSums to obtain the UNCONDITIONAL du Bois-Reymond theorem: ∃ f : C(𝕋), the Fourier series of f diverges at 0.

Strengthen the divergence to a residual/comeagre set of functions (the Banach–Steinhaus condensation-of-singularities form): the set of continuous functions with divergent Fourier series at 0 is comeagre in C(𝕋).
